sections.title: Introduction to Angle Grading
sections.content: Gonioscopy remains the clinical gold standard for evaluating the iridocorneal angle. Accurate grading is crucial for differentiating between open-angle and angle-closure glaucomas, identifying risk factors for primary angle closure (PAC), and determining the necessity of laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI). While Shaffer's system is widely used for its simplicity, Spaeth's system provides a more granular anatomical description.

rows: Only Schwalbe's Line (+/- top of TM)

sections.title: The Spaeth System: (A) Iris Insertion
content: A (Anterior): Iris inserts anterior to Schwalbe's line.
B (Behind): Iris inserts posterior to Schwalbe's line but anterior to the Scleral Spur.
C (Scleral Spur): Iris inserts at the Scleral Spur.
D (Deep): Iris inserts into the Ciliary Body Band.
E (Extremely Deep): Iris inserts into the Scleral Wall/deep Ciliary Body.
Note: Parentheses (e.g., (D)) indicate the insertion seen upon indentation gonioscopy.

sections.title: The Spaeth System: (B) Angular Width
sections.content: This is the angle formed by a line tangential to the inner surface of the trabecular meshwork and a line tangential to the iris surface about one-third of the way from the periphery. It is recorded in degrees (e.g., 10°, 20°, 30°, 40°).

rows: Steep rise from insertion (often in high insertions)
Iris follows a straight plane from insertion

content.explanation: From Posterior to Anterior (Deep to Superficial): I (Iris), C (Ciliary Body Band), S (Scleral Spur), T (Trabecular Meshwork), S (Schwalbe's Line).

sections.title: Gonioscopy Red Flags
content: Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS) bridging the angle
Neovascularization of the Angle (NVA) crossing Scleral Spur
Sampaolesi Line (pigment on or anterior to Schwalbe's Line)
Double Hump Sign on indentation (Plateau Iris)
Blood in Schlemm's Canal (Elevated EVP/Sturge-Weber)

sections.title: The Dynamic Gonioscopy Process
content: Step 1: Patient Selection - Ensure topical anesthesia and no recent surgery/trauma.
Step 2: Lens Choice - Use a Zeiss/Sussman four-mirror lens for indentation (no coupling gel) or Goldmann lens for stability.
Step 3: Dim the Lights - Minimize miosis; use a short, narrow slit beam avoiding the pupil to prevent false opening.
Step 4: Primary View - Identify the most posterior structure visible without manipulation.
Step 5: Indentation - Apply gentle pressure to the cornea to force aqueous into the angle, distinguishing appositional from synechial closure.
Step 6: Documentation - Record Grade (Shaffer or Spaeth), Pigment (0-4+), and abnormalities (NVA/PAS).

branches: Scleral Spur: Attachment for Ciliary Muscle
Ciliary Body Band: Dull gray/brown band
Iris Processes: Fine extensions from iris to TM
Pupillary Block: Most common; aqueous trapped behind iris
Plateau Iris: Anteriorly positioned ciliary processes
Lens-Induced: Phacomorphic (large lens) or Ectopia Lentis
Posterior Pushing: Suprachoroidal hemorrhage or Effusion
Anterior Pulling: PAS from inflammation or NVA

sections.title: Surgical/Laser Decision Algorithm
content: 1. Perform Gonioscopy: Identify Grade 0-2 or ITC (Iridotrabecular Contact).
2. Dynamic Gonioscopy: Is it appositional? (Opens with pressure).
3. Assess Risk: High IOP, PAS, or symptomatic?
4. Intervention: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) for pupillary block.
5. Post-LPI Gonioscopy: If angle remains narrow, consider Plateau Iris or Phacomorphic components.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: Always check the 'worst' quadrant (usually superior) as it is typically the narrowest.
Use the '10 o'clock/2 o'clock' rule for PAS: they are usually broader and higher than iris processes.
In Spaeth's system, 'D40f' describes a wide, deep, flat angle—the 'ideal' open angle.
Plateau iris is suggested when the angle is narrow but the central AC is deep.

sections.title: Recent Advances: AS-OCT vs. Gonioscopy
sections.content: While Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT) provides objective, reproducible measurements of the Angle Opening Distance (AOD) and Trabecular Iris Space Area (TISA), it cannot distinguish between appositional and synechial closure as effectively as dynamic gonioscopy. AS-OCT is an excellent screening tool but does not replace the expert clinical assessment of the Spaeth system.

sections.content: The definitive guide to anterior chamber angle assessment, transitioning from clinical suspicion to precise, evidence-based gonioscopic grading for glaucoma management.

sections.title: Anatomy: The Angle Landmarks (Schwalbe to Ciliary Body)
content: 1. Schwalbe's Line: Termination of Descemet's membrane.
2. Non-pigmented Trabecular Meshwork: Posterior to Schwalbe's.
3. Pigmented Trabecular Meshwork: Primary site of aqueous outflow.
4. Scleral Spur: The most anterior projection of the sclera; attachment site of the ciliary muscle.
5. Ciliary Body Band: The vascularized, darker, most posterior structure visible.

sections.title: Gonioscopy Red Flags
content: Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS)
Iris processes masking the angle
Neovascularization of the angle (NVA)
Blood in Schlemm's Canal (high episcleral venous pressure)
Exfoliation material on the trabecular meshwork

content.mnemonic: I Can See The Scleral Spur
content.explanation: I (Iris) - C (Ciliary Body) - S (Scleral Spur) - T (Trabecular Meshwork) - S (Schwalbe's Line). Posterior to Anterior.

sections.title: Technique: Dynamic Gonioscopy
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic; ensure patient is upright or supine.
Step 2: Apply gonioscopy lens (e.g., Goldmann 3-mirror or Posner 4-mirror) with viscoelastic coupling agent.
Step 3: Keep the beam narrow and vertical (1-2mm width) to avoid light-induced pupil constriction.
Step 4: Use indentation (compression) gonioscopy to differentiate appositional from synechial closure.
Step 5: If angle opens under compression, the closure is appositional (potential for LPI).

sections.title: Recent Advances: Imaging vs. Gonioscopy
content: AS-OCT (Anterior Segment OCT): Non-contact, high resolution (5-10 microns). Useful for objectively measuring AOD500 (Angle Opening Distance at 500 microns).
UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy): 35-50 MHz frequency. The gold standard for visualizing structures behind the iris (e.g., ciliary cysts, ciliary body position).
Note: Gonioscopy remains the clinical gold standard as it allows for direct observation of pigment and PAS that OCT may miss.
